Where does AI’s view of the world come from?

Researchers from Harvard gave a large language model the same questions from the World Values Survey that were put to nearly 94.000 people in 65 countries, then compared its answers with theirs. The model’s responses were closest to people from Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic (WEIRD) societies, and the further a country was culturally from the United States, the less the model’s answers resembled its people’s. The authors point to the training data, much of it scraped from the internet, which comes disproportionately from WEIRD societies because people elsewhere are less likely to be online (Atari et al., 2023).

Now question the map itself. Each dot is a whole country, but Indonesia and Australia are not single cultures. Each contains many regions, languages, communities and ways of life, and one dot hides all of that. The survey, and the researchers who chose how to analyse it, also see the world from somewhere. Whose view of the world does this map show, and whose does it leave out?

This program sits within Indonesia’s Pembelajaran Mendalam (Deep Learning) approach to mindful, meaningful and joyful learning (Kementerian Pendidikan Dasar dan Menengah, 2025), and within national guidance that positions AI as a support that does not replace the teacher (BSKAP, 2025).

What kind of teacher do you want your PPG students to become, and what should AI never take away?

Before we talk about AI, start with your own work

Think about a recent teaching, mentoring or teacher-education task that took more time than you wanted, or that was difficult to get right for all learners. It might have involved explaining a difficult idea, creating examples, adapting a resource, preparing questions, giving feedback, or planning for learners with different levels of readiness.

Now imagine that an AI system offered to help. Where would you welcome that help, and where would you hesitate?

Write down one task from your own context where AI might be useful, and one part of that task that you would not want to hand over to a system.

Notes are saved on this device only.

Keep these two notes. We will return to them during the live session. The purpose is not to decide whether AI is good or bad. It is to begin from the work you already do, the learners you know, and the professional judgement you already use.

Why this matters now

Generative AI is already being used to produce explanations, lesson materials, examples, images, feedback and assessment support. It can produce useful material very quickly, but the same fluency that makes it attractive can also make weak, inaccurate or inappropriate output look convincing.

For educators, the central issue is therefore not simply whether AI can produce something. The question is whether the output is accurate, appropriate for the learner, aligned with the intended learning, safe to use, and worth using at all.

Research on AI literacy distinguishes basic understanding of how AI systems operate from the ability to use them competently in context. In education, that competency depends on professional judgement, because AI systems do not independently understand curriculum intent, learner needs or the consequences of educational decisions (Chiu, 2025; Miao & Holmes, 2023).

Quick self-check

Before continuing, rate yourself from 1 (not yet confident) to 5 (very confident):

I can explain, in simple terms, how generative AI produces a response.
I can recognise when a fluent AI response may still be unsuitable for teaching.
I can decide what information I should and should not provide to an AI system.
I can identify a teaching task where AI could support, rather than replace, professional judgement.

There is no required score. The purpose is to make your starting point visible to you.

Concept 1: What generative AI is, and what it is not

Try it first

Open a generative AI tool of your choice. Ask it to explain a concept that you know well and that is relevant to your work. Keep the prompt deliberately simple, for example: “Explain fractions to a Year 5 student”, “Explain persuasive writing”, or an equivalent concept from your own teaching area.

Read the response once, then note:

What is happening here?

Generative AI systems produce output by predicting likely continuations from patterns learned from very large datasets. They can generate fluent text, images and other content, but fluency is not the same as understanding. The system does not independently know whether an explanation is factually correct, whether it matches your intended curriculum, whether it is suitable for your learners, or whether it reflects the cultural and educational context in which you work.

These limitations also raise ethical questions. If some languages, communities or perspectives are less well represented in the data behind an AI system, its apparently neutral output may not represent all learners equally. We will return to questions of bias, representation and fairness later in the programme.

This is why AI output should be treated as a draft or suggestion rather than as an authority. A response can be well written and still be wrong, incomplete, overgeneralised or poorly matched to the teaching purpose. AI literacy therefore includes recognising both capability and limitation, and knowing when human expertise must take control (Chiu, 2025).

A useful way to think about this is human-in-the-loop practice. AI can generate, suggest or reorganise material, but the educator remains responsible for deciding what is accepted, revised or rejected. Human judgement is not a final check added after the “real” work of AI. It is part of the educational process itself (Memarian & Doleck, 2024; Miao & Holmes, 2023).

Literacy, Competency and Human-AI Partnership

Check your first response again

Return to the AI explanation you generated. Identify the specific professional knowledge you used to judge it. Was it subject knowledge, knowledge of learners, curriculum knowledge, cultural knowledge, assessment knowledge, or something else?

Concept 2: Prompting is the expression of professional intent

Improve the same task

Use the same concept again, but this time give the AI more information. Include the learner group, the purpose of the explanation, the form you want the response to take, and one or two constraints that matter in your context.

For example, instead of “Explain fractions”, you might ask for an explanation for learners who can identify halves and quarters but are beginning to compare unlike fractions, using one everyday example and avoiding formal fraction algorithms.

Compare the first and second outputs. Which became more useful? Which problems remained?

Clearer prompts do not remove judgement

A prompt is simply the information and instruction we provide to the system. Better prompting can make an output more relevant because we have made more of our professional intent explicit. It can specify audience, purpose, constraints, language level, structure or the kind of examples we want.

However, clearer prompting does not make an AI system authoritative. It does not guarantee factual accuracy, curriculum alignment or pedagogical quality. The educator still needs to verify the content and decide whether it is worth using.

This distinction matters because “prompt engineering” can easily be treated as the main skill. In education, the more important skill is making good professional decisions about purpose, context and quality. The prompt is one way of communicating those decisions to the system.

A practical prompting pattern

When you want AI to support a teaching task, make four things clear:

  • Context - who are the learners and what is happening?
  • Purpose - what do you want the material to help achieve?
  • Constraints - what must the response preserve, avoid or include?
  • Review - what will you check before deciding whether to use it?

Try revising your prompt one more time using this pattern. Do not aim for a perfect output. Aim for an output that gives you something useful to judge and work with.

Concept 3: Purposeful and responsible educational use

Choose a real educational problem

Return to the task you identified at the start. Before using AI, state the educational problem in one sentence. For example: “My learners understand the idea orally but struggle with the reading level of the available text”, or “My preservice teachers can describe the strategy but struggle to adapt it for different levels of learner readiness.”

Now decide what role, if any, AI could play. You might ask it to generate alternative explanations, worked examples, practice questions, multiple representations, possible formative questions, or a draft resource to be reviewed.

Use AI once for that task, then judge the output using the questions below.

Judge the educational value, not just the output

  • Purpose: Does this actually address the educational problem?

  • Accuracy: Is the content correct and defensible?

  • Learner: Is it appropriate for these learners, at this point in their learning?

  • Context: Does it make sense in this cultural, institutional and classroom context?

  • Safety: Have I avoided sharing information that should not be given to the system?

  • Learning: Does the AI support learning, or has it done the important thinking for the learner?

  • Judgement: What must I change, verify or reject before use?

Some of these questions are also ethical questions: who benefits, who might be excluded or misrepresented, what information is shared, how AI use is disclosed, and where responsibility remains. A later module will examine these issues explicitly.

AI can support access and differentiation when it changes the pathway to learning while preserving the learning intention. It can also support teachers in generating examples, questions, possible next steps or draft feedback. But it should not be treated as a substitute for the educator's evaluative judgement, and it should not make decisions about learners that require professional accountability.

The same principle applies to learner data. Removing a name does not automatically make information safe to share. Combinations of details can still identify a person (Rocher et al., 2019). Use approved systems and local policy where learner information is involved, and minimise what is shared.

The aim is not to use AI wherever possible. The aim is to use it where it adds educational value while keeping the teacher and the learner central to the decision.

As the programme develops, we will return to these boundaries in greater depth, particularly questions of bias, cultural and linguistic representation, privacy, equity of access, transparency and responsible use.
